lessons.title: What Are Plains?
lessons.notes_html:
Plains are one of the major landforms on Earth. They are found on every continent and cover more than one-third of the world's land area. A plain is a vast expanse of relatively flat land with low relief — there is only a small difference in elevation across it.

Physical Features of Plains

  • The landscape is flat or gently sloping.
  • Relief is low, with little to no hills or mountains.
  • Plains are often intersected by rivers and their river valleys.
  • Soils are frequently fertile, because plains are formed by sediments deposited by rivers or glaciers.
  • Plains often support grassland ecosystems, helped by favourable climate and fertile soil.

Plains Around the World

  • Steppe — the temperate grasslands of Asia and eastern Europe, which receive little rain and grow grass instead of trees.
  • Savana — grasslands with scattered trees, found in Africa, Australia and South America.
  • Tundra — in the Arctic region, the plains of frozen ground.
  • Indus Plain — in Pakistan, known for its fertile soil.
  • West Siberian Plain — one of the world's largest and flattest plains, covering almost 1 million square miles (2.6 million km2).
  • Prairie Plains — with rich soil and favourable climate, often called breadbaskets because they produce so much food.
  • The Nile River flows through the Egyptian Plain and makes it fertile; Egypt is called the Gift of the Nile.

Key Points

  • Plains are flat, low-relief land covering more than one-third of the world's land area.
  • Steppe, Savana and Tundra are plains known by special names in different regions.

lessons.title: Plains and Other Landforms
lessons.notes_html:
Plains can be told apart from mountains, plateaus and valleys by their relief and shape:

LandformMain feature
PlainA flat area of land that is mostly level, with little to no hills or mountains
MountainHas high relief with steep slopes
PlateauHas a relatively flat or undulating surface raised above the surrounding land
ValleyA low area of land between hills or mountains

How Plains Are Formed: Two Broad Groups

  • Erosional plains — formed by the wearing down of land by natural agents such as water, wind or glaciers. Over time these agents wear the land down, smooth out irregularities and create a relatively flat surface.
  • Depositional plains — formed by material carried and deposited by running water, wind or glaciers. They are characterised by rich, fertile soil that supports agriculture and so contributes to the economy of the country.

On the basis of formation, the unit groups plains broadly into these two types: erosional and depositional.

Key Points

  • A plain is level and low; a mountain is high and steep; a plateau is flat but raised; a valley lies between hills.
  • Erosional plains are worn flat; depositional plains are built up by deposits.

lessons.title: The River System
lessons.notes_html:
A river system is a network of interconnected rivers and their tributaries. A tributary is a fresh water channel that feeds the main river.

Main Components of a River System

  • Source — the starting point from which water flows and sets the course of the whole river system.
  • Tributaries — smaller streams or rivers that flow into the main river.
  • Main channel — the central pathway through which the river flows.
  • Drainage basin (watershed) — the entire area of land drained by a river and its tributaries.
  • River valley — the low-lying area on either side of a river.
  • Floodplain — the flat land beside the river that is flooded at times of high-water flow.
  • River delta — the landform at the mouth of the river, where it meets a body of water such as an ocean or a lake.

Two Great Rivers

  • The Nile River in Africa is the longest river in the world, about 6,650 kilometres (4,130 miles) long, flowing through eleven countries. It is in Egypt.
  • The Amazon River in South America is the largest river in the world in terms of water volume.

Key Points

  • A river system = source, tributaries, main channel, drainage basin, river valley, floodplain and delta.
  • The Nile is the longest river; the Amazon carries the most water.

lessons.title: Three Courses of a River
lessons.notes_html:
From source to mouth, a river passes through three courses:

CourseCharacterMain features
Upper courseSteep gradients, fast-flowing water, narrow channels; erosion is dominantV-shaped valleys, waterfalls, rapids, gorges
Middle courseAlso called the mature or valley stage; gradient is less steep, water flows more slowlyMeanders, ox-bow lakes, flood plains, natural levees, braided channels
Lower courseAlso called the delta or old age stage; the river mainly deposits sediment instead of erodingDeltas, distributaries, estuaries

Why a Delta Forms in the Lower Course

A delta is a triangle-shaped landform at the mouth of a river. In the lower course the gradient (slope) decreases, so the velocity of the river falls. The slower river can no longer carry its load, so it deposits the sediments it brought from the upper and middle courses, and this deposition builds the delta. For example, the Indus River falls into the Arabian Sea and forms a delta. The Ganges Delta is the world's largest delta.

Importance of the Middle Course

The middle course combines the benefits of water supply, transportation, energy generation, ecology and recreational value, sustaining ecosystems and human activities.

Importance of Rivers

  • For biodiversity: rivers provide diverse habitats, water, shelter and food for fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, and act as corridors for the movement and migration of species. Rivers are called the lifelines of the Earth.
  • For the economy: rivers give fresh water for people, agriculture and industries; their fertile floodplains and deltas give rich soil for farming; river transport is cost-effective and environment friendly and supports trade; flowing water supports hydropower generation; and rivers attract tourists for boating, fishing, rafting and wildlife watching.

Key Points

  • Upper course erodes (V-shaped valleys, waterfalls); middle course makes meanders and flood plains; lower course deposits (deltas).
  • Deltas form because the river slows down in its lower course and drops its sediment.

lessons.title: Major Sources of Water
lessons.notes_html:
Water keeps everything alive, supports nature, controls the weather and keeps temperatures balanced. The major sources of water on Earth are classified into three categories:

  • Surface water — water found on the surface of the Earth.
  • Ground water — water stored under the Earth's surface.
  • Atmospheric water — water in the atmosphere, which returns as precipitation.

Only about 2.5% of the Earth's water is freshwater. The oceans are the largest source of water, holding about 97% of the Earth's water, but ocean water is saline and not directly suitable for most uses; it can be purified by the Reverse Osmosis Process. Ocean water also gives seafood, supports fisheries and shipping, regulates climate by absorbing and distributing heat, and can be used for renewable energy.

Key Points

  • Water sources are of three kinds: surface, ground and atmospheric.
  • Oceans hold about 97% of all water, but it is salty.

lessons.title: Surface Water
lessons.notes_html:
Surface water is water found on the surface of the Earth in lakes, rivers, streams and reservoirs, both freshwater and saline. Only a little more than 1.2% of all freshwater is surface water, yet it serves most of life's needs.

Rivers

Rivers collect water from many sources and carry it towards oceans or other water bodies. The Amazon River is in South America, the Nile is in Africa and the Yangtze is in Asia. Pakistan depends mainly on the Indus River system, which originates in the Himalayas and gives water for irrigation, hydropower and domestic use. The Indus Basin Irrigation System is an extensive network of main canals, branch canals and distributaries.

Lakes and Reservoirs

  • Lakes are large bodies of water usually surrounded by land; reservoirs are human-made storage areas created by damming rivers. Both give water for drinking, irrigation and hydroelectric power.
  • Lake Superior in North America is the largest freshwater lake in the world.
  • Lake Manchar, west of the Indus River in Sindh, is the largest freshwater lake in Pakistan and one of the largest in Asia; its area changes with the seasons, from about 350 km2 to 520 km2.

Wetlands and Glacial Meltwater

  • Wetlands — marshes, swamps and bogs where water covers the soil for a significant part of the year. They act as natural filters, purify water and provide habitats for many species.
  • Glaciers are moving ice masses formed where temperatures stay below freezing and snow accumulates. In northern Pakistan, the Siachen, Baltoro and Biafo glaciers provide much water when they melt in the warmer months.

Key Points

  • Rivers, lakes, reservoirs, wetlands and glacial meltwater are the surface-water sources.
  • Lake Superior is the world's largest freshwater lake; Lake Manchar is Pakistan's largest.

lessons.title: Groundwater and Atmospheric Water
lessons.notes_html:
Groundwater is water stored under the Earth's surface. It is refilled when rainwater and surface water soak into the ground. In Pakistan people use groundwater a lot, especially in dry areas, through wells and tubewells for drinking, irrigation and industry.

Springs and Aquifers

  • Springs occur when groundwater emerges naturally onto the Earth's surface, where the water table intersects the land surface. Hot springs are popular tourist attractions and centres for medical therapy and recreation.
  • Aquifers are underground layers of water-bearing permeable rock. They act as natural reservoirs and supply water to wells and springs.

Water Scarcity in Pakistan

Pakistan faces challenges of water scarcity and management because of population growth, climate change and inefficient water usage practices. Sustainable management of water sources is crucial to meet the growing demand, maintain ecological balance and reduce the impacts of climate change.

Atmospheric Water

Precipitation — rain, snow and hail — is a primary source for replenishing both surface water and groundwater. The water cycle, driven by evaporation, condensation and precipitation, ensures a continuous supply of water to these sources.

Key Points

  • Groundwater is stored in aquifers and reaches the surface through wells and springs.
  • Population growth, climate change and wasteful use cause water scarcity in Pakistan.

lessons.title: Precipitation and the Water Cycle
lessons.notes_html:
Precipitation is any form of water that falls from the atmosphere to the surface of the Earth. It occurs when water vapour turns into droplets during condensation; the droplets join, become heavy and fall under gravity. Precipitation replenishes surface water and groundwater, sustains ecosystems and helps regulate the global climate.

Types of Precipitation

  • Rain — the most common type; it forms when water droplets in the atmosphere become large enough to fall. Raindrops are typically 0.5 to 5 millimetres in diameter. Rain is of three kinds: orographic rain (also called relief rain), convectional rain and frontal rain.
  • Snow — forms when the temperature in the atmosphere is below freezing point and water vapour turns directly into ice crystals that join to form snowflakes.
  • Sleet — forms when raindrops fall through a layer of freezing air near the ground; the drops have a hard outer layer with cold water inside.
  • Dew — moisture that forms on grass, leaves and metal objects during the cool hours of night or early morning, when surface temperatures drop below the dew point; it is an important moisture source for plants in dry areas.
  • Hail — solid ice pellets or balls formed when strong updrafts in thunderstorm clouds carry raindrops up into extremely cold air, where they freeze and gain layers of ice until they are too heavy and fall.

The Water Cycle

The water cycle, also known as the hydrological cycle, is the continuous process by which water circulates between the surface of the Earth, the atmosphere and back again. Its key processes are:

  • Evaporation — liquid water changes into water vapour and rises into the atmosphere.
  • Transpiration — plants absorb water through their roots and release water vapour from their leaves into the atmosphere.
  • Condensation — water vapour cools and changes back into liquid water, forming clouds.
  • Sublimation — ice or snow turns directly into water vapour without melting into liquid, as on glaciers and high mountain peaks.
  • Precipitation — water falls back as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
  • Runoff — precipitation that flows over the land into rivers, lakes and oceans.
  • Infiltration — precipitation that seeps into the ground and becomes groundwater in aquifers.

Key Points

  • Rain is the most common precipitation; orographic rain is also called relief rain.
  • The water cycle (hydrological cycle) runs through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, sublimation, precipitation, runoff and infiltration.

lessons.title: Sewage Waste, Water Purification and Biogas
lessons.notes_html:
Sewage waste (wastewater) is the used water from domestic, industrial and commercial activities. It contains harmful pathogens, bacteria, viruses and parasites, so it must be treated before use.

The Sewage Treatment Process

Wastewater is carried away, screened, and passed through primary treatment, secondary treatment and final treatment. The treated water is then returned to rivers, the solids are returned to land, and power is generated.

Uses of Treated Sewage Waste

  • To irrigate agricultural fields, landscaping and urban green spaces — this conserves freshwater.
  • For industrial purposes such as power plants, manufacturing facilities and cooling systems.
  • To recharge groundwater by putting it into aquifers or wells.
  • For non-potable uses in buildings, such as toilet flushing, washing and cleaning.
  • For recreation in designated areas, such as boating and fishing.

Water Purification Methods

  • Boiling — heating water to its boiling point (100°C) kills bacteria, viruses and parasites.
  • Filtration — passing water through cloth, sand or a commercial filter removes sediment and some microorganisms.
  • Chlorination — adding chlorine to water to kill bacteria and viruses; it is commonly used in public water supply systems.
  • Solar disinfection (SoDIS) — filling clear bottles with water and leaving them in direct sunlight for at least 6 hours; the ultraviolet rays kill germs.
  • Purification tablets — tablets containing chlorine or iodine disinfect the water.
  • Distillation — heating water into steam and condensing the steam to collect purified water, removing bacteria, viruses and minerals.

Biogas — the Greener Fuel

Biogas is a green energy produced from organic waste such as food scraps, animal manure and plant residues. Its main component is methane gas, a clean-burning fuel, so biogas is called the Greener Fuel. It can be used for cooking, heating and generating electricity. It is renewable, produces fewer greenhouse gases, reduces dependence on fossil fuels and turns waste into something useful.

Key Points

  • Treated sewage water can irrigate fields, serve industry and recharge groundwater.
  • Boiling, filtration, chlorination, solar disinfection and distillation purify water.
  • Biogas, whose main component is methane, is the Greener Fuel.

lessons.title: What Is a Settlement?
lessons.notes_html:
In the beginning, man lived in isolation and later started living in communities, moving from place to place (nomadism). The first settlements were closely linked to the discovery and practice of agriculture: as humans learned to cultivate crops and domesticate animals, they settled in one place for longer periods, and permanent settlements formed. This change from nomadism to a settled lifestyle was a major turning point in human history, around 10,000 BCE.

A settlement is a community or a place where people reside and engage in various activities, such as living, working and interacting with one another. Settlements primarily serve as places of residence for people.

The First Civilisations

The oldest recorded civilisation in the world is the Mesopotamian Civilisation, between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers (the name means the land between the rivers). The first civilisations developed on river banks: the Egyptians on the Nile, the Mesopotamians on the Tigris and Euphrates, the ancient Chinese on the Yellow River and ancient India on the Indus.

Key Points

  • Man first lived in isolation, then in communities; permanent settlements began with agriculture.
  • A settlement is a place where people live, work and interact.

lessons.notes_html:
People settle where conditions favour human habitation. The unit identifies these suitable conditions:

  • Availability of water — a nearby reliable source such as a river, lake or underground water, for drinking, cooking and agriculture.
  • Topography and land — the topography of a location plays a vital role in settlement suitability. Flat or gently sloping land suits construction, agriculture and infrastructure; steep slopes, flood-prone areas and landslide-prone areas pose challenges.
  • Suitable climate — moderate temperatures, sufficient rainfall and suitable growing seasons are preferred; extreme heat, cold or excessive rainfall pose challenges.
  • Natural resources — fertile soil for agriculture, forests for timber and fuel, minerals for economic activities and renewable energy sources.
  • Transportation and accessibility — nearness to roads, railways or waterways, and to nearby towns, cities and markets.
  • Security and safety — low crime rates, nearness to emergency services and adequate measures against natural disasters.
  • Social and community factors — a sense of community, access to healthcare, educational institutions, recreational spaces and cultural amenities.
  • Economic opportunities — job opportunities, markets, trade routes and a favourable business environment. Historical and cultural factors may also influence settlement patterns.

Key Points

  • Water, flat land, good climate, resources, transport, safety, community facilities and jobs make a place suitable for settlement.
  • Topography plays a vital role in settlement suitability.

lessons.title: Rural Settlements and Hamlets
lessons.notes_html:
There are two types of settlements: rural and urban. Rural settlements are characterised by low population density, are typically located in rural or agricultural areas, and are associated with farming, agriculture and primary industries.

Forms of Rural Settlements

  • Clustered settlements — houses are located close together, forming a cluster; often found where resources such as water or fertile land are concentrated.
  • Dispersed settlements — houses are spread out over a larger area, each located independently with clear distances between them.
  • Linear settlements — elongated in shape, following a road, river or coastline, so houses are arranged in a line.
  • Nucleated settlements — a central core or nucleus, such as public buildings or markets, surrounded by scattered houses or agricultural land.

Hamlets

Hamlets are small, compact settlements with a limited number of houses. They are often found in remote or isolated areas, where the population is small and primarily engaged in agriculture or other traditional livelihoods.

Advantages and Disadvantages of Rural Settlements

  • Advantages: natural environment, community and social bonds, lower cost of living, reduced noise and pollution, and connection with nature.
  • Disadvantages: limited employment opportunities, lack of infrastructure and services, limited access to resources, social isolation, and distance from urban centres.

Key Points

  • Rural settlements are small, low-density and agriculture-based; they may be clustered, dispersed, linear or nucleated.
  • A hamlet is a small, compact settlement with a limited number of houses.

lessons.title: Urban Settlements and Settlements of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Urban settlements are large, densely populated areas with a high concentration of people, buildings and infrastructure, usually associated with industrial, commercial and service-oriented activities. They range from small towns to major cities. Urban settlements often function as centres of commerce and trade.

Advantages and Disadvantages of Urban Settlements

  • Advantages: employment opportunities, infrastructure and services, cultural and social activities, educational opportunities and efficient public transportation.
  • Disadvantages: higher cost of living, overcrowding and lack of space, pollution, increased crime rates, and stress and lifestyle challenges.

Suburban settlements lie on the outskirts of urban areas, with a mix of residential, commercial and industrial zones, giving a residential environment close to urban facilities.

Major Types of Settlements in Pakistan

  • Major cities — Karachi (commercial hub), Lahore (cultural centre), Islamabad (capital city).
  • Villages — small, spread-out communities centred on agriculture, across Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan.
  • Metropolitan areas — large urban centres with expansive suburbs and high economic activity; Karachi is an economic powerhouse and a metropolitan area.
  • Small towns — local trade and service hubs, such as Faisalabad (industrial town) and Sialkot (textile and sports goods).
  • Hill stations — mountain settlements with cool climate, popular for tourism, such as Murree and Quetta.
  • Port cities — Karachi (main seaport) and Gwadar (developing port city).
  • Desert towns — adapted to desert conditions, such as Tharparkar and Cholistan.
  • Agricultural settlements — farm-based communities, such as Multan and Sargodha (citrus farming).
  • Strategic settlements — near borders or strategic points, such as Skardu and Chaman (border town with Afghanistan).

Key Points

  • Urban settlements are large, dense and based on industry, commerce and services.
  • Karachi is Pakistan's commercial hub, main seaport and a metropolitan area.

lessons.title: Functions of Settlements, Towns and Cities
lessons.notes_html:
Functions of a Settlement

  • Residential — settlements primarily serve as places of residence, providing housing and infrastructure.
  • Commercial — centres of commerce and trade, with markets, shops and malls.
  • Industrial — factories, manufacturing plants and industrial zones where goods are produced or processed.
  • Administrative — government offices, administrative buildings and public institutions.
  • Educational — schools, colleges and universities.
  • Recreational and cultural — parks, gardens, theatres, museums and sports facilities.
  • Transport and communication — roads, railways, airports and ports, and communication networks.
  • Agricultural — in rural settlements, farmland where crops are grown, livestock is raised and products are processed.

Towns and Cities Compared

FeatureTownCity
Size and populationRelatively smaller; lower populationLarger; higher population
Infrastructure and servicesBasic infrastructure; limited servicesAdvanced infrastructure; wide range of services including healthcare, education and entertainment
Economic activitiesLimited rangeDiverse range; more employment and business opportunities
TransportationRelatively simpler systemsMore complex networks, including public transportation

Conurbation and Megapolis

  • A conurbation is an extended urban area formed by the merging of adjacent cities or towns, when separate urban areas grow and blend together into a continuous built-up area, with high population density and strong interaction between its parts.
  • A megapolis is an even larger and more extensive urban region: a vast metropolitan area encompassing multiple cities, towns and suburbs, often spanning different administrative boundaries or even multiple states or provinces, with a massive population and extensive infrastructure networks.

Time Zones

A time zone is a region of the Earth that follows a uniform standard time. The Earth is divided into 24 time zones, each about 15 degrees of longitude wide, with the Prime Meridian (0 degrees longitude) as the reference. Pakistan Standard Time is set at 75.08° E longitude.

Key Points

  • Settlements perform residential, commercial, industrial, administrative, educational, recreational, transport and agricultural functions.
  • A conurbation is merged neighbouring cities; a megapolis is a still larger urban region of many cities and suburbs.

lessons.title: Origins of Agriculture
lessons.notes_html:
Human life initially relied on gathering and hunting for food. The advent of agriculture brought a drastic change, as humans domesticated plants and animals. Around 10,000 years ago, agricultural communities emerged — this is known as the First Agricultural Revolution or Neolithic Revolution. Agriculture is the practice of cultivating crops, rearing animals and related activities to produce food, fibre and other products that sustain human life.

Oasis Theory

The Oasis Theory suggests that agriculture arose in response to climate changes, during the transition from the Ice Age to the present epoch. Global warming led to glacier retreat and the formation of oases in arid regions. These oases attracted plants and animals and provided a reliable food source. Humans settled near the oases, which led to the domestication of plants and the emergence of agriculture.

River Valleys Theory

The River Valleys Theory (Hydraulic Civilization Theory) proposes that agriculture originated in river valleys because of favourable conditions such as water supply and fertile soil, which led to human settlement and flourishing cultivation. Examples are the valleys of the Nile, Tigris, Euphrates, Indus and Yellow River.

Key Points

  • Early humans gathered and hunted; farming began about 10,000 years ago in the Neolithic Revolution.
  • The Oasis Theory links the start of agriculture to climate change; the River Valleys Theory links it to water and fertile soil.

lessons.title: Types of Agriculture
lessons.notes_html:
Almost 38.5 percent of the global workforce is engaged in the agriculture sector. Agriculture has two main branches: crop cultivation and livestock farming. Based on different factors, agriculture can be broadly categorised as follows:

  • Subsistence agriculture — farming to meet the needs of the farmer's family or local community, using traditional methods, with limited surplus for sale. It is common in rural areas of Pakistan, particularly the northern regions, where farmers grow wheat, rice, maize and vegetables.
  • Intensive agriculture — maximises land productivity through advanced techniques and high inputs; practised in densely populated areas with limited arable land, for example high-yielding rice varieties cultivated intensively in the Punjab region of Pakistan.
  • Extensive agriculture — practised in areas with abundant land and limited labour, with low inputs; it includes livestock grazing and large-scale crop cultivation, as in the USA, Canada, Russia and Brazil.
  • Commercial agriculture — produces crops and livestock for sale in the market to generate profit, with large-scale operations, advanced technology and high inputs; cash crops include cotton, coffee, soybeans and wheat.
  • Mixed farming — cultivating crops and rearing livestock on the same farm, to diversify income and improve stability and sustainability.
  • Truck farming — also called market gardening: cultivating vegetables, fruits and flowers that have high demand in local markets or can be transported quickly to urban areas.
  • Livestock farming — raising animals for products such as milk and meat; it plays a crucial role in rural livelihoods.

Key Points

  • About 38.5% of the world's workforce works in agriculture.
  • Subsistence farming feeds the family; intensive farming uses high inputs on little land; extensive farming uses low inputs on much land; commercial farming produces for the market.

lessons.title: Methods of Farming
lessons.notes_html:
Traditional and Conventional Methods

  • Agroforestry — intentionally planting trees on farms to provide shade, a better microclimate, windbreaks, erosion control and additional income from timber, fruits, nuts and fodder; it improves biodiversity and soil health.
  • Crop rotation — growing different crops in a specific sequence on the same piece of land over a defined period, to improve soil health, manage pests and use nutrients better.
  • Mixed cropping or intercropping — growing two or more different crops simultaneously on the same piece of land; it gives efficient use of resources, better pest and disease management, improved soil health and increased biodiversity.
  • Polyculture — growing multiple crops together in the same field, usually without a specific spatial arrangement, with a diverse range of crops such as grains, vegetables, fruits and herbs and no dominant crop.
  • Monoculture — cultivating a single crop species on a given piece of land over a significant area, often with specialised machinery and inputs; it makes management and harvesting efficient but increases vulnerability to pests and diseases, soil degradation and reduced biodiversity.

Modern Methods

  • Organic agriculture — avoids synthetic chemicals such as pesticides and fertilisers, and relies on compost, crop rotation and natural pest control; it protects the environment and soil health and focuses on animal welfare.
  • Sustainable agriculture — farming that meets current needs without harming the environment or depleting resources for future generations, balancing food production with care for soil, water, biodiversity and farming communities.

Evaluating Agricultural Projects

Projects are evaluated by methods such as cost-benefit analysis, impact assessment, performance indicators, field surveys, benchmarking, cost-effectiveness analysis and participatory evaluation — checking crop production, money saved or earned, and effects on the environment and community.

Key Points

  • Polyculture grows many crops in one field; monoculture grows only one.
  • Organic farming avoids synthetic chemicals; sustainable farming protects resources for future generations.

lessons.title: Pakistan — an Agricultural Country
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan has a varied climate, primarily arid, with hot summers and cool to cold winters. Irrigation is crucial: the country has an extensive infrastructure of dams, canals and tube wells, and canal irrigation from the Indus River system is the primary water source, ensuring year-round cultivation.

Agriculture in Pakistan's Economy

  • Agriculture is the backbone of the economy: it contributes about 18.9% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), accounts for 42.3% of the employed labour force, and is the largest source of foreign exchange earnings.
  • Total arable land in Pakistan was 40.12% in 2020 (World Bank, unit text page 55), and it is declining due to rapid urbanisation. Note: the unit's Key Points box (page 65) prints almost 42.12% instead — the two figures in the book do not match; the unit text figure, 40.12%, is the one used here.
  • Major crops (wheat, rice, cotton and sugarcane) contribute around 4.18% and minor crops 2.1% to GDP.
  • The livestock sector contributes 11% to GDP and employs approximately 35 million people; fisheries and forestry each contribute an estimated 0.4%.
  • Agriculture provides raw materials to major industries: textile, leather, rice processing, edible oil, sugar and food processing.
  • Pakistan is among the world's top ten producers of wheat, cotton, sugarcane, mango, dates and kinnow oranges, and is ranked 10th in rice production.
  • Punjab is the major agricultural province, where wheat and cotton are the most grown; 60% of the agricultural share of exports comes from Punjab.

Key Points

  • Agriculture contributes about 18.9% of Pakistan's GDP and employs 42.3% of its labour force.
  • Arable land was 40.12% in 2020 by the unit text; livestock contributes 11% of GDP.

lessons.title: Crops of Pakistan and Farming Raw Materials
lessons.notes_html:
Crops by Season

Rabi cropsKharif crops
SeasonSown and harvested in winter, typically October/November to March/AprilSown in the monsoon summer season, around June/July to September/October; rain-fed, relying on abundant rainfall and warmer temperatures
ExamplesWheat, barley, grams, mustard, potatoesRice, cotton, maize, sugarcane, millet

By purpose, crops are cash crops (cotton, tobacco, sugarcane, tea, oilseeds — grown for commercial value) and fodder crops (alfalfa, maize fodder, berseem, lucerne — grown for feeding livestock).

Major Crops

  • Wheat — the largest crop in terms of production in Pakistan and the most important staple, grown in Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; average annual production is around 25–27 million metric tons.
  • Rice — mainly in Punjab and Sindh, including the famous Basmati; around 7–8 million metric tons annually.
  • Cotton — an important cash crop known as Silver Fiber, grown in Punjab and Sindh; around 10–12 million bales annually, each bale weighing 170 kg.
  • Sugarcane — mainly in Punjab and Sindh, grown for sugar, molasses and ethanol; around 60–70 million metric tons annually.
  • Maize (corn) — concentrated in Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Sindh; around 5–6 million metric tons annually.
  • Fruits — mangoes (the king of fruits; almost 2 million metric tons in 2022), citrus fruits, apples, bananas, guavas, dates and grapes. Vegetables (potatoes, tomatoes, onions and others), pulses (lentils, chickpeas, beans) and oilseeds (sunflower, canola, sesame) are also cultivated.

Impacts of Livestock Farming on the Environment

Cattle farming drives deforestation; it is a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions (methane and nitrous oxide); it uses substantial water and can cause water scarcity; overgrazing leads to land degradation and soil erosion; improper management of animal waste pollutes water and air; and expanding cattle farming destroys natural habitats and biodiversity. Sustainable practices are needed to reduce these impacts.

Raw Materials from Farming and Fishery

  • There are two types of raw materials from farming: crop-based raw materials (food grains, fruits, vegetables and oilseeds; animal feed such as corn, soybeans and alfalfa; biofuel materials; and fibre such as cotton for the textile industry) and livestock-based raw materials (meat and dairy products, leather and hides, wool and fibres).
  • Fishery raw materials come from marine and freshwater sources and support the seafood industry, fish meal and fish oil, fish processing and aquaculture.
  • Using these raw materials generates revenue and supports employment, trade and economic development in rural and coastal communities. International institutions such as the FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations) support agricultural development with finance, technical expertise and fair trade.

Key Points

  • Rabi crops are winter crops; Kharif crops are monsoon summer crops.
  • Wheat is Pakistan's largest crop by production; cotton is called Silver Fiber.
  • Farming gives two types of raw materials: crop-based and livestock-based.

lessons.title: Climate Change and the IPCC
lessons.notes_html:
Climate change refers to the long-term changes in the Earth's weather patterns and temperatures. It is caused by natural processes and by human activities, such as burning fossil fuels (like coal, oil and gas) and cutting down forests, which release gases that trap heat in the atmosphere. The trapped heat warms the Earth.

What Climate Change Does

  • It raises temperatures and changes weather patterns, bringing more extreme weather events like storms, floods and droughts.
  • It melts ice in the polar regions and raises sea levels, affecting coastal areas and the creatures that live there.
  • It affects plants, animals and ecosystems; some species find it difficult to survive in their usual habitats, and biodiversity is lost.

The IPCC

IPCC stands for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the United Nations body for assessing the science related to climate change. The IPCC reports that the Earth's average surface temperature has risen by about 1.1 degrees Celsius since the late 19th century, mainly due to human activities such as burning fossil fuels. About 750 billion tons of ice is melting every year due to global warming. To address climate change we must reduce greenhouse gas emissions — by using renewable energy, conserving energy and planting trees.

Key Points

  • Climate change is the long-term change in weather patterns and temperatures.
  • IPCC = Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change; the Earth has warmed by about 1.1°C since the late 19th century.

lessons.title: The Greenhouse Effect
lessons.notes_html:
The greenhouse effect is a natural process in the atmosphere of the Earth. The Earth receives heat from the Sun in the form of sunlight. Some of this heat is absorbed by the surface of the Earth — land, water and trees. When the surface is heated, it releases some heat radiation.

Certain gases in the atmosphere, like carbon dioxide and methane, act like the glass walls of a greenhouse: they trap some of the heat radiated from the surface, warming the atmosphere and making it a comfortable place for us to live. The greenhouse effect is important for life because it keeps our planet warm enough for us to survive.

From Greenhouse Effect to Global Warming

Human activities, such as burning fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas, release extra amounts of these greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. This causes an imbalance in the natural greenhouse effect and increases the temperature of the Earth. This increase is called global warming. Too much of the greenhouse effect causes climate change, rising sea levels and extreme weather events.

Key Points

  • Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat like the glass of a greenhouse.
  • Extra gases from burning fossil fuels cause global warming.

lessons.title: Changes Caused by the Greenhouse Effect and the Ozone Layer
lessons.notes_html:
Changes Caused by the Greenhouse Effect

  • Global warming — increased greenhouse gases raise the Earth's temperature, causing weather changes, ice melting and ecosystem disruptions.
  • Climate change — extreme weather like heatwaves, droughts, hurricanes and heavy rainfall, with significant impacts on agriculture, water resources and human settlements.
  • Rising sea levels — melting ice sheets and glaciers add water to the oceans, threatening coastal areas with erosion and flooding and displacing coastal communities.
  • Extinction of species — loss of biodiversity affects ecosystem health and functioning.
  • Impact on agriculture — changes in temperature, rainfall patterns and extreme weather can reduce crop yields, disrupt food production and affect food security and the economy.
  • Health effects — heatwaves cause heat-related illnesses and stress, and climate change favours disease-carrying organisms like mosquitoes, increasing the risk of vector-borne diseases such as dengue fever.

The Ozone Layer

The ozone layer is a special part of the atmosphere of the Earth that acts like a shield. It is located in the stratosphere, at about 10 to 50 kilometres above us, and is made up of ozone gas — three oxygen atoms (O3) bonded together. It protects us from the harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays of the Sun, which can cause sunburn, skin cancer, eye diseases and other problems.

Causes of Ozone Depletion

Ozone depletion is mainly caused by human-made chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other ozone-depleting substances, commonly used in aerosol sprays, air conditioners, refrigerators and foam insulation. When released, they rise to the ozone layer, are broken down by sunlight, and release chlorine and bromine atoms that destroy ozone molecules — one chlorine or bromine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. The Montreal Protocol, an international agreement adopted on 16 September 1987, limits the production and use of ozone-depleting substances, and the ozone layer is slowly recovering.

Key Points

  • A stronger greenhouse effect brings warming, extreme weather, rising seas, species loss, farm losses and health risks.
  • The ozone layer in the stratosphere shields us from UV rays; CFCs deplete it.

lessons.title: Main Causes of Climate Change and Going Green
lessons.notes_html:
Main Causes of Climate Change

The greenhouse effect and the resultant global warming are the main causes of climate change. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide act like a blanket, trapping some heat instead of letting it escape into space and making the Earth a habitable planet. Human activities — burning fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas) for energy, deforestation and certain industrial processes — have increased these gases, thickening the blanket and trapping more heat. Global warming then brings rising temperatures, melting ice caps and glaciers, rising sea levels, changes in precipitation patterns, and more frequent and severe storms and heatwaves. Pakistan is the 6th most vulnerable country to climate change.

Practices for a Green Future

  • Reduce, Reuse, Recycle (the 3Rs) — reduce waste by opting for reusable items like water bottles, shopping bags and coffee cups; reuse items by donating or repurposing clothes and furniture; recycle paper, plastic and glass to reduce the need for new resources.
  • Conserve energy — turn off lights and appliances when not in use, use energy-efficient bulbs and appliances, adjust thermostats, unplug chargers, and use natural light. Conserving energy reduces our carbon footprint and lowers greenhouse gas emissions.
  • Use renewable energy — install solar panels, use wind turbines, and support policies that promote renewable energy.
  • Conserve water — take shorter showers and turn off the tap while brushing teeth; fix leaks in faucets or pipes promptly; collect rainwater for gardening and outdoor use; use water-efficient appliances and fixtures.
  • Plant trees and support green spaces — join tree planting initiatives, create gardens at home or school, and support reforestation organisations; planting trees has numerous environmental benefits.
  • Choose sustainable transportation — walk or cycle for short distances, use public transportation, carpool, and choose electric or hybrid vehicles when possible.
  • Support local and sustainable products — such as organic food or environment friendly household items.

Key Points

  • Greenhouse gases thickened by fossil fuels, deforestation and industry are the main cause of climate change.
  • The 3Rs, saving energy and water, renewable energy, tree planting and clean transport build a green future.

lessons.title: Minerals and Their Types
lessons.notes_html:
Minerals are naturally occurring, solid substances with a specific chemical composition and a unique crystalline structure, formed over long periods through geological processes. Feldspar is the most abundant mineral in the Earth's continental crust, and silicate minerals form more than 90% of the crust.

Why Minerals Matter

  • They are essential raw materials for various industries.
  • Mining and processing create employment opportunities.
  • They bring revenue through taxes, royalties and export earnings, and can be valuable exports.
  • They help diversify an economy and are essential for technological advancement.
  • Mineral resources must be managed sustainably and responsibly, keeping environmental and social impacts in balance.

Types of Minerals

  • Metallic minerals — contain metallic elements, have a lustrous appearance and are good conductors of heat and electricity; for example iron ore, copper, gold, silver, lead and zinc. They are important for construction and manufacturing, and are classified as ferrous and non-ferrous minerals.
  • Ferrous minerals — contain iron as their main component; they are dark and magnetic, and iron is vital for industries like construction and transportation.
  • Non-ferrous minerals — do not contain iron as their main constituent; examples are copper, aluminium, lead, zinc, tin and gold.
  • Non-metallic minerals — do not contain metals; they are used in construction, ceramics, glass manufacturing, agriculture and cosmetics.

Key Points

  • Minerals are natural, solid substances with a definite chemical composition.
  • Iron ore, copper, gold, silver, lead and zinc are metallic minerals; metallic minerals divide into ferrous (with iron) and non-ferrous (without iron).

lessons.title: Types of Mining
lessons.notes_html:
Different mining methods are used to extract minerals, depending on where the mineral lies:

  • Hand-Panning Mining — a traditional method of manually extracting gold from rivers and streams using a shallow pan, swirling sediment in water to separate gold from lighter materials; simple and small-scale.
  • Open-cast Mining — extracting minerals from the surface by removing the overlying layers of soil and rock, creating a large open excavation; used when the mineral lies close to the surface, for coal, copper, gold and iron ore.
  • Shaft Mining — extracting minerals from deep beneath the Earth's surface by creating vertical tunnels or shafts; used for gold, silver and various metal ores, with specialised equipment for safety and efficiency.
  • Adit Mining — also known as horizontal mining or level mining: a horizontal tunnel, called an adit, is driven into the side of a hill or mountain to reach the minerals; it offers cost-effectiveness and safety, and is used for limestone and various metal ores.
  • Drill Mining — also known as drilling and blasting: holes are drilled in the rock and filled with explosives, which are detonated to break the rock and extract the mineral; used in underground and open-pit mining for gold, copper and other ores.
  • Long-wall Mining — miners dig a long, narrow tunnel underground and use a big machine to cut a slice of coal from the wall, while special supports keep the roof from falling; when all the coal is removed, the roof is allowed to collapse slowly and the space is filled in.
  • Surface Mining — the top layers of soil and rock are removed to access minerals beneath, using large machines like draglines and shovels in an open pit; after mining, the site is restored by replacing the soil and replanting vegetation.

Key Points

  • Adit mining is horizontal, into a hillside; shaft mining is vertical, deep underground.
  • Hand-panning is the traditional manual method of extracting gold.

lessons.title: Minerals Found in Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Metallic Minerals

  • Copper — found in Qalat, Zhob and Chagai district of Balochistan (the Saindak Copper-Gold Project is a major operation) and in Dir, Chitral and Hazara in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Copper is used in construction, electrical wiring, coins and electronics.
  • Iron ore — mainly in the Chiniot and Kalabagh regions of Punjab. The Kalabagh deposit is one of the largest in the country, with measured reserves of 350 million tonnes. Iron ore is also found in Domal Nisar (Chitral), Langrial (Abbottabad) and Chilghazi (Chaghi). It is used in steel production for construction and manufacturing.
  • Chromite — primarily in Balochistan (Muslim Bagh, Chaghi, Kharan, Khuzdar) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Mohmand Agency); used in stainless steel, alloys and refractory materials.

Non-Metallic Minerals

  • Rock salt — Pakistan has extensive salt reserves, particularly in the Khewra Salt Mine, one of the largest and oldest salt mines in the world; the salt is known as Himalayan pink salt and is used in the chemical industry and cooking. Other reserves are at Kalabagh, Warcha and Bahadurkhail.
  • Limestone — major reserves in Daudkhel, Wah, Rohri, Hyderabad, Sibi, Dera Ghazi Khan, Kohat, Nowshera and Khuzdar; used in cement, the chemical industry and construction.
  • Gypsum — mainly in Khewra, Dandot, Daudkhel, Qadirabad, Rohri, Kohat, Dera Ghazi Khan, Loralai and Sibi; used for plastering, cement production and as a soil amendment.

Mineral-Rich Areas

  • Punjab — the Salt Range with the Khewra Salt Mine; Chiniot and Kalabagh (iron ore); Khushab (uranium).
  • Balochistan — Chagai and Reko Diq (copper and gold); Lasbela (barytes, gypsum, limestone, bentonite); Killa Saifullah (chromite and copper); Harnai, Kalat and Barkhan (coal); Loralai and Chaghi (marble).
  • Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — Swat Valley (emeralds); Dir (marble and nephrite); Mansehra (granite, marble, nephrite, graphite); Chitral.
  • Sindh — the Thar Desert, with vast lignite coal deposits for the country's energy needs.
  • Gilgit-Baltistan — Nagar and Shigar, known for precious gemstones like emeralds, rubies and sapphires, plus phosphates, quartz and marble.

Some Rare Minerals

Pakistan's rare minerals include Peridot, a green gemstone from the Kohistan region; Imperial Topaz, a pink variety of topaz mined in Mardan District; the unique blue K2 Azurite from the K2 region; and spinel, aquamarine, apatite, serpentine and Paprok tourmaline from different regions.

Key Points

  • Kalabagh is one of Pakistan's largest iron deposits (350 million tonnes); Khewra is one of the largest and oldest salt mines in the world.
  • Saindak (copper-gold), Thar (coal) and Nagar and Shigar (gemstones) are famous mineral areas.

lessons.title: Power Resources, Alternative Energy and Coal-Mining Risks
lessons.notes_html:
Fossil Fuels and Thermal Power

Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — are commonly used to generate power in various industries and for electricity production; they run thermal power stations. They are important because of their abundant availability, high energy content and established infrastructure, but their use causes air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Thermal power projects named in the unit include Port Qasim (Karachi), Sahiwal Coal, Jamshoro, Muzaffargarh, Faisalabad Gas, Balloki (Kasur), Nandipur (Gujranwala), Bhikki (Sheikhupura), Hub (Balochistan) and Guddu Thermal Power Plants.

Industries Related to Minerals and Power

  • Mineral-related industries: construction (limestone, granite, marble), cement (limestone, clay, gypsum), glass (silica sand), steel (iron ore), ceramic (clay, feldspar, quartz), fertilizer (phosphates and sulfur) and jewelry (precious and semi-precious gemstones such as emeralds, rubies and sapphires).
  • Power-related industries: power generation using fossil fuels, hydropower, wind and solar energy; the oil and gas industry; coal-fired thermal plants; and transmission and distribution, which deliver electricity to homes and businesses.

Alternative Sources of Energy

  • Solar energy — solar panels or photovoltaic cells convert sunlight into electricity without harmful emissions; the Quaid-e-Azam Solar Power Park has been installed in Bahawalpur district of Punjab.
  • Wind energy — wind turbines harness the wind to generate electricity; wind farms can produce large amounts of power, and wind plants can be installed in Sindh Province and in Lasbela and Gwadar districts of Balochistan.
  • Hydropower — the force of flowing or falling water drives turbines to produce electricity; Pakistan has several hydropower projects such as the Tarbela Dam and Mangla Dam.
  • Biomass energy — energy derived from organic materials such as agricultural waste or wood, burned or converted into biofuels to produce heat or electricity; for example, agricultural waste like sugarcane biogas can be used as a fuel in biomass power plants.

These sources are renewable and sustainable: they reduce greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution, conserve natural resources, have a smaller ecological footprint, and create new jobs.

Risk Factors in Coal Mining

  • Cave-ins, explosions and equipment failures can cause accidents and injuries to miners.
  • Exposure to coal dust, silica and toxic gases can lead to respiratory diseases and black lung disease.
  • Coal mining contributes to land degradation, deforestation, water pollution and greenhouse gas release.
  • Underground mining can cause mine collapses, endangering miners and damaging infrastructure.
  • Accumulation of methane gas, a byproduct of coal, can lead to explosions if not properly controlled.
  • Miners face physical strain from working in challenging conditions with heavy loads, and coal mines are susceptible to fires that release toxic fumes.

Strict safety measures, adequate training and regular monitoring are needed to reduce these risks.

Key Points

  • Coal, oil and natural gas are the fossil fuels used for power; solar, wind, hydropower and biomass are the cleaner alternatives.
  • Coal mining risks include cave-ins, explosions, methane gas, dust diseases, fires and environmental damage.
